curriculum.source: NCERT Class XI Chemistry Part I

learning_units.title: Chemistry and the Nature of Matter
learning_units.short_description: Connect chemistry to life, then build a clear particle-level picture of matter, its states, mixtures, elements, and compounds.

concepts.title: Scope and Meaning of Chemistry
Alchemy, Iatrochemistry, and the Development of Modern Chemistry
Contributions of Ancient Indian Chemistry
Chemistry in Life, Industry, Health, Materials, and the Environment
Matter: Mass and Occupied Space
Particle Arrangement in Solids, Liquids, and Gases
Interconversion of States by Temperature and Pressure
Macroscopic Classification of Matter
Mixtures, Pure Substances, and Physical Separation
Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Mixtures
Elements, Compounds, Atoms, and Molecules

skills: Explain the scope of chemistry in simple language.
Recognise major contributions to the development of chemistry.
Connect chemistry to familiar applications in life and society.
Compare the particle arrangement and observable behaviour of solids, liquids, and gases.
Classify common substances as elements, compounds, homogeneous mixtures, or heterogeneous mixtures.
Explain why mixtures can be separated physically while compounds require chemical methods.
practice: Complete at least 6 recall, explanation, classification practice items.
learning_units.why_it_matters: This opening unit gives chemistry a purpose and establishes the language of matter, particles, mixtures, elements, and compounds used throughout the chapter.
learning_route: Connect chemistry to familiar changes, materials, health, industry, and the environment.
Build a particle-level picture of solids, liquids, gases, and changes of state.
Classify samples as mixtures or pure substances, then as elements or compounds.
Use a short explanation and classification check to confirm the foundation.
mastery_criteria: Explain what chemistry studies without relying on a memorised sentence.
Name at least three areas in which chemistry improves life or technology.
Distinguish the historical development of chemistry from the modern scientific discipline.
Explain the three states of matter using particle arrangement and movement.
Predict the effect of heating, cooling, or pressure on a change of state.
Correctly classify unfamiliar examples as mixture, pure substance, element, or compound and justify the choice.

learning_units.title: Measurement and Reliable Chemical Data
learning_units.short_description: Measure matter with correct units, then handle scientific notation, uncertainty, significant figures, conversions, density, and temperature reliably.

ncert_sections.title: Properties of Matter and their Measurement

ncert_subtopics.title: Properties of Matter and their Measurement

concepts.title: Physical and Chemical Properties
Quantitative Measurement as a Number with a Unit
SI Base Units, Derived Quantities, and Prefixes
Mass, Weight, and Laboratory Measurement
Volume Units and Measuring Apparatus
Density as Mass per Unit Volume
Celsius, Fahrenheit, and Kelvin Scales
Scientific Notation for Very Large and Small Numbers
Arithmetic with Scientific Notation

Precision and Accuracy
Significant Figures in Calculations and Rounding

skills: Distinguish physical properties from chemical properties.
Select appropriate SI units and prefixes for a quantity.
Convert common mass, volume, density, and temperature units.
Use laboratory measurement vocabulary and apparatus correctly.
Calculate density, mass, or volume when the other two values are known.
Write and interpret numbers in scientific notation.
Apply the correct arithmetic rule to numbers in scientific notation.
Count significant figures and round a result appropriately.
Distinguish precision from accuracy using experimental data.
Build and cancel unit factors to perform dimensional analysis.
practice: Complete at least 12 formula, calculation, application, error analysis, unit conversion practice items.
learning_units.why_it_matters: Every later numerical answer depends on choosing valid measurements, carrying units, and reporting only the precision the evidence supports.
learning_route: Separate physical and chemical properties, then match quantities to SI units and measuring tools.
Use mass, volume, density, and temperature conversions in short examples.
Represent data with scientific notation and interpret uncertainty, precision, and accuracy.
Apply significant figures, rounding, and dimensional analysis to calculation checks.
mastery_criteria: Choose correct SI units for the seven base quantities and common derived quantities.
Explain the difference between mass and weight and between physical and chemical properties.
Convert between common volume and temperature scales without losing units.
Solve density calculations and state the result with an appropriate unit.
Convert ordinary numbers to and from scientific notation and perform the four basic operations correctly.
Identify significant figures in varied values, including zeros and exact counted quantities.
Round calculated answers using the rule appropriate to the operation.
Explain whether a set of measurements is precise, accurate, both, or neither.
Complete a multi-step unit conversion with units cancelling visibly at each step.

learning_units.title: Chemical Combination Laws and Dalton's Theory
learning_units.short_description: Use experimental mass and gas-volume patterns to understand the laws of chemical combination and the atomic model Dalton built from them.

ncert_sections.title: Gay Lussac's Law of Gaseous Volumes

ncert_subtopics.title: Gay Lussac's Law of Gaseous Volumes

concepts.title: Law of Conservation of Mass
Law of Definite Proportions
Law of Multiple Proportions
Gay Lussac's Law of Gaseous Volumes
Avogadro's Law
Experimental Origin of Dalton's Atomic Theory
Dalton's Four Postulates
What Dalton's Theory Explains and Where It Falls Short

skills: State each law in precise but student-friendly language.
Identify which law is illustrated by a simple mass or gas-volume data set.
Use small whole-number ratios to explain multiple proportions and gaseous volumes.
Distinguish laws based on mass from laws based on gas volume.
State and explain Dalton's postulates.
Connect specific postulates to laws of chemical combination.
Describe why Dalton's theory could not fully explain gaseous-volume relationships or why atoms combine.
practice: Complete at least 7 recall, data interpretation, application, explanation, comparison practice items.
learning_units.why_it_matters: The combination laws provide the experimental evidence, and Dalton's theory turns that evidence into the particle model needed for masses, moles, and reactions.
learning_route: Identify the mass and gas-volume patterns behind the five laws of chemical combination.
Distinguish the laws by applying them to compact data examples.
Connect the laws to Dalton's postulates in their conceptual order.
Use the model to explain the evidence while recognising its historical limits.
mastery_criteria: State all five laws and distinguish them by the quantity each law compares.
Identify the correct law from unfamiliar experimental data and justify the choice.
Calculate and interpret the simple whole-number ratio in a multiple-proportion or gas-volume example.
Explain each Dalton postulate in the student's own words.
Link conservation of mass and fixed composition to the relevant postulates.
Name at least one limitation without dismissing the model's historical value.

learning_units.title: Masses of Atoms and Molecules
learning_units.short_description: Use the carbon-12 standard, isotopic abundance, and chemical formulae to calculate atomic, average atomic, molecular, and formula masses.

concepts.title: Relative Atomic Mass, Carbon-12 Standard, and Unified Mass Unit
Average Atomic Mass from Isotopic Abundance
Molecular Mass from a Molecular Formula
Formula Mass for Ionic and Non-Molecular Substances

skills: Explain why atomic masses are relative and what one unified mass unit represents.
Calculate a weighted average atomic mass from isotope data.
Calculate molecular mass from a molecular formula.
Choose formula mass instead of molecular mass for an ionic solid and calculate it correctly.
practice: Complete at least 6 formula, calculation, comparison practice items.
learning_units.why_it_matters: Atomic and molecular masses are the bridge between chemical formulae and measurable amounts of substance.
learning_route: Use carbon-12 to understand relative atomic mass and the unified mass unit.
Calculate average atomic mass from isotopic abundance.
Find molecular and formula masses from chemical formulae.
mastery_criteria: Explain the carbon-12 reference and use u correctly.
Calculate average atomic mass from isotope abundances with correct weighting.
Calculate molecular and formula masses from unfamiliar formulae.
Explain why NaCl has a formula mass rather than a molecular mass.

learning_units.title: Mole, Molar Mass, and Composition
learning_units.short_description: Connect particles to measurable amounts with the mole and molar mass, then use composition data to derive empirical and molecular formulae.

concepts.title: Mole as the SI Unit of Amount of Substance
Avogadro Constant and Specified Elementary Entities
Atoms, Molecules, Ions, Electrons, and Formula Units as Entities
Molar Mass and its Relation to Atomic, Molecular, and Formula Mass
Conversions among Mass, Moles, and Number of Entities
Mass Percentage of Elements in a Compound
Empirical Formula as the Simplest Whole-Number Ratio
Molecular Formula from Empirical Formula and Molar Mass

skills: Identify the elementary entity represented by one mole of a substance.
Use the Avogadro constant with correct powers and units.
Relate mass in u to molar mass in grams per mole.
Convert in both directions among mass, moles, and number of entities.
Calculate the mass percentage of each element in a compound.
Use percentage data to obtain moles and a simplest whole-number ratio.
Derive an empirical formula without prematurely rounding ratios.
Use empirical-formula mass and molar mass to determine a molecular formula.
practice: Complete at least 12 formula, calculation, unit conversion, application, multi step problem practice items.
learning_units.why_it_matters: This unit links microscopic entities to laboratory mass and then turns measured composition into defensible chemical formulae.
learning_route: Treat the mole as a count of specified entities and connect it to the Avogadro constant.
Convert among particles, moles, mass, and molar mass with explicit units.
Calculate percentage composition from a chemical formula.
Turn composition data into empirical and molecular formulae using a transparent mole-ratio method.
mastery_criteria: Explain why one mole always contains the same number of specified entities.
State the entity being counted for an element, molecule, ion, or ionic compound.
Move accurately among grams, moles, and entities in multi-step questions.
Write every conversion with an appropriate unit and sensible significant figures.
Calculate elemental mass percentages from a correct chemical formula.
Explain the difference between empirical and molecular formulae.
Derive an empirical formula from percentage or mass data using a transparent sequence of steps.
Determine a molecular formula from empirical formula and molar mass and verify that the multiplier is a whole number.

learning_units.title: Stoichiometry and Solution Calculations
learning_units.short_description: Read a balanced equation as a quantitative map, solve reaction and limiting-reagent problems, and express solution concentration correctly.

concepts.title: Balancing Chemical Equations without Changing Formula Subscripts
Stoichiometric Coefficients and Mole Ratios
Mass, Mole, Particle, and Gas-Volume Relationships
Limiting Reagent and Maximum Product
Amount of Substance in a Solution
Mass Per Cent of a Solution
Mole Fraction
Molarity, Dilution, and Temperature Dependence
Molality and Temperature Independence
Using Density to Convert between Concentration Measures

skills: Balance a chemical equation by changing coefficients only.
Interpret coefficients as particle, mole, mass, and gas-volume relationships where valid.
Use a mole ratio to calculate a required reactant or expected product.
Identify the limiting reagent and calculate the maximum product formed.
Calculate mass per cent, mole fraction, molarity, and molality.
Use dilution and density relationships while keeping volume and solvent-mass definitions distinct.
practice: Complete at least 12 balancing, calculation, multi step problem, application practice items.
learning_units.why_it_matters: Stoichiometry turns a chemical equation into a practical calculation tool and integrates nearly every quantitative idea learned earlier in the chapter.
learning_route: Balance the chemical equation and read its mole relationships.
Convert known amounts into moles before applying the stoichiometric ratio.
Identify a limiting reagent and calculate the amount of product.
Apply stoichiometry to molarity, molality, mole fraction, and mass percentage.
mastery_criteria: Balance unfamiliar chemical equations without changing any formula subscript.
Translate a balanced equation into mole and mass relationships with units shown.
Solve a limiting-reagent problem and explain why the identified reactant limits product formation.
Choose the correct concentration expression from the information given and apply its exact definition.
Solve multi-step solution problems involving dilution or density and check whether the final magnitude and unit are sensible.
